title: Finding Your Rhythm
use_cases: Use when reviewing a draft to identify repetitive phrasing or clunky transitions
Implement when mimicking stylistic choices of established authors to improve flow
Configure when applying musical structures like verses and choruses to narrative pacing
content:
Look, there’s no magic formula. Rhythm is feel. It’s a vibe. The best advice is to stop just writing and start listening. To your own work, and to the work of others.

1. Read Aloud: Read your draft into your phone’s voice memos. Listen back while you’re driving or doing the dishes. You will hear every clunky phrase, every repeated word, every place the rhythm dies. It’s excruciating but necessary.
2. Transcribe Your Faves: Type out a few pages from an author whose prose you adore. Don’t just copy-paste. Physically type it. You’ll start to feel their rhythmic choices in your own fingers. It’s like learning a guitar solo by playing it note for note.
3. Listen to Music: Pay attention to the structure of songs. Notice how a verse builds to a chorus, how a bridge changes the energy before returning to the hook. Your chapters, paragraphs, and even sentences can learn from this.

Your draft is just a demo track. You’re the producer. Go back into the studio and start mixing.
